items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public authorities law and the public service law, in
relation to establishing a highway and depot charging action plan
items.lawCode: Add §1885, amd §1020-gg, Pub Auth L; add §121-b, Pub Serv L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4830

SPONSOR: KENNEDY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public authorities law and the public service law,
in relation to establishing a highway and depot charging action plan

 
PURPOSE:

This legislation amends the public authorities and public service laws
to require the development of a highway and depot charging action plan
to meet the state's clean transportation goals.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1. Sets for the legislative findings.

§ 2. Adds § 1885 to the public authorities law to:

(1)require NYSERDA, in consultation with the Department of Transporta-
tion, Department of Motor Vehicles, New York State Thruway Authority,
New York Power Authority, Long Island Power Authority, Department of
Environmental Conservation and the electric distribution and trans-
mission utilities to develop a highway and depot charging action plan
within nine months of the effective date of the bill and every three
years thereafter. The charging action plan shall support and complement
DOT planning for fast charger deployment along alternative fuel corri-
dors; identify the number and location of fast chargers along priority
highway corridors; estimate future need for such deployment for the
purposes of specified parameters; identify the number and location of
highway charging hubs; estimate total charging capacity required to
serve light-, medium- and heavy-duty electric vehicles at each highway
charging hub through at least 2050; identify, to the extent practicable,
the number and location of commercial and public fleet vehicles in oper-
ation; identify the number and location of fleet charging zones; esti-
mate future need for charging deployment and charging capacity in the
fleet charging zones; and seek to optimize fast charger deployment among
the highway charging hubs and charging development among the fleet
charging zones to reduce the cost of interconnection, electric distrib-
ution, and local transmission upgrades while serving projected vehicle
traffic volumes.

(2) direct NYSERDA to develop a stakeholder engagement process to raise
consumer awareness and education and solicit feedback from the public,
representatives or residents of environmental justice or disadvantaged
communities, electric vehicle manufacturers, electric vehicle supply
equipment manufacturers, fleet operators, and others.  To the extent
practicable and consistent with applicable timelines, NYSERDA may coor-
dinate the highway and depot charging action plan stakeholder input
process with the process set forth in § 1884 of the public authorities
law.

(3) direct NYSERDA to submit the highway and depot charging action plan
to the public service commission no later than nine months after the
effective date of § 1885 and an updated charging plan every three years
thereafter. The charging plan shall be made publicly available on
NYSERDA's website.

(4) require NYSERDA to facilitate development of a fast charging network
along priority highway corridors by designating locations as highway
charging hubs in accordance with specified parameters.

( 5 ) require NYSERDA to prioritize geographic areas for designation as
fleet charging zones based on specified parameters.

(6) set forth definitions for terms used in § 1885.

§ 3. Adds § 121-b of the public service law to:

(1) require the Public Service Commission, in consultation with New York
State Thruway Authority, New York Power Authority, and the Long Island
Power Authority, within 90 days of submission of a highway charging
action plan or depot charging action plan, to commence a proceeding to
direct New York electric utilities to produce capital plans to develop,
own and operate interconnection, electric distribution and local trans-
mission upgrade necessary to meet charging capacity requirements at all
highway charging hubs. The capital plans shall include upgrades to site
interconnection at all highway charging hubs; be designed to minimize
the need for multiple or duplicative upgrades at a given site by consid-
ering specified parameters and, where feasible, be designed as future-
proofing upgrades; prioritize interconnection, electric distribution and
local transmission upgrades at thruway charging hubs; consider the
existence of relevant commitments from site and/or charging operators in
prioritizing the schedule of upgrades; and identify a schedule for
upgrades, subject to reasonable constraints.

(2) direct that all investments in the utility capital plan shall be
recovered by the utilities through a proceeding established by the
Commission, a petition filed by one or more utilities, or the utility
rate case process. The Commission may establish an appropriate mechanism
for site owners or operators to contribute to the cost of identified
upgrades, such as but not limited to a contribution from charging reven-
ue at the site.

(3) direct the Commission to ensure upgrades are implemented in a timely
and cost-effective manner to meet identified charging requirements. The
Commission may evaluate the benefits of proposed upgrades in accordance
with, among others, certain specified factors.

(4) require electric utilities, in establishing the capital plan, to
evaluate benefits of utilizing distributed energy resources such as
energy storage or managed charging programs.

(5) define "future-proofing upgrades."

(6) authorize the Commission, in consultation with the commissioner of
environmental conservation, to issue rules and regulations for the
purposes of carrying out the provisions of the section.

(7) require the Commission, in a proceeding established in accordance
with section (1) of this section or in another proceeding designated by
the Commission, to consider certain specified factors, among others, to
identify and remove barriers to the efficient and timely deployment of
charging infrastructure needed to electrify New York's commercial and
public fleet vehicles on the fleet charging zones.

§ 4. Amends § 1020-gg of the public authorities law to require the Long
Island Power Authority (LIPA) to establish or amend an existing capital
plan to implement upgrades in its service territory in accordance with a
proceeding implemented by the public service commission pursuant to §
121-b of the public service law. LIPA and NYSERDA shall identify no
fewer than two highway charging hubs in LIPA's service territory where
future-proofing upgrades shall be implemented on a similar timeline as
at the thruway charging hubs defined in § 1885 of the public authorities
law.

§ 5. Establishes the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

New York has set rigorous goals - such as the Climate Leadership and
Community Protection Act of 2019 (CLCPA), Advanced Clean Trucks and
Advanced Clean Cars II rules, and the Zero Emissions Vehicles sales
targets - to predominantly electrify its transportation sector by 2050,
with significant target deadlines rapidly approaching. To meet the clean
transportation goals we have set, New York must now commit to equally
rigorous and well-planned goals to expedite electric grid transmission
and distribution infrastructure and interconnection upgrades. Fast
charging stations need to be built all along the New York State Thruway
and other high priority corridors. But fast chargers create considerable
demand for energy; exponentially more demand than currently required to
power the gas pumps found at Thruway rest stops and throughout the
state. As a result, as sales of zero emission vehicles continue to grow
and gain momentum, the electric grid must grow just as quickly to keep
pace with demand.  Electric grid infrastructure upgrades are costly and
subject to a time-consuming process that requires considerable coordi-
nation to plan, engineer, permit, and construct. That extensive process
must begin now - far ahead of the electrification tar get deadlines - to
meet the demands that will emerge with those deadlines. In fact, if the
upgrade process fails to outpace the time when electric vehicle adoption
reaches scale, we will not have a reliable and adequate electric supply
to power all the new electric vehicles on New York's roadways.

This legislation establishes the framework to proactively plan for elec-
tric vehicle fast-charging deployment on New York's highways by direct-
ing NYSERDA, in consultation with the Department of Transportation,
Department of Motor Vehicles, New York State Thruway Authority, New York
Power Authority, Long Island Power Authority, Department of Environ-
mental Conservation and the electric distribution and transmission util-
ities to, among other things, identify the number of fast chargers,
highway charging hubs, and fleet charging zones currently in operation
and in development along New York's priority highways, estimate future
need for fast charger deployment, and estimate total charging capacity
required through at least 2050. This planning will include stakeholder
input in line with existing energy planning processes, and NYSERDA will
then report the plan to the public service commission to effectuate it
through a proceeding that requires New York's electric utilities to
produce appropriate capital plans.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:
TBD.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

BILL NUMBER: S4830A

SPONSOR: KENNEDY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public authorities law and the public service law,
in relation to establishing a highway and depot charging action plan

 
PURPOSE:

This legislation amends the public authorities and public service laws
to require the development of a highway and depot charging action plan
to meet the state's clean transportation goals.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Sets forth the legislative findings.

§ 2: adds § 1885 to the public authorities law to (1) require NYSERDA,
in consultation with relevant state agencies and authorities and the
electric utilities, to develop a highway and depot charging action plan,
the parameters of which are specified, and to update such plan every
three years; (2) directs NYSERDA to develop a stakeholder engagement
process which may be coordinated with the existing stakeholder engage-
ment process set forth in section 1884 of the public authorities law;
(3) directs NYSERDA to submit the charging plan to the PSC no later than
nine months after the effective date of this section; (4) requires
NYSERDA et al to facilitate development of a fast charging network along
priority highway corridors by designating locations as highway charging
hubs according to specified parameters; (5) requires NYSERDA et al to
prioritize geographic areas to be designated as fleet charging zones
based on specified parameters; and (6) defines terms.

§ 3: adds § 66-v of the public service law to (1) require the Public
Service Commission, in consultation with relevant authorities, to
commence a proceeding within 90 days of receiving the highway and depot
charging action plan, to direct New York electric utilities to produce
capital plans, in accordance with specified parameters, to develop, own
and operate interconnection, electric distribution, and local trans-
mission upgrades necessary to meet charging capacity requirements at all
highway charging hubs identified in the charging plan; (2) direct the
Commission to reduce costs to utility customers by considering mech-
anisms including but not limited to funding made available by the state
and/or federal government, to develop a plan to ensure cost-effective-
ness of investments in the capital plan, and to consider benefits made
available to utility customers through such investments; (3) direct the
Commission to ensure upgrades are implemented in a timely and cost-ef-
fective manner to meet charging requirements at all identified highway
charging hubs and fleet charging zones and to evaluate the benefits of
proposed upgrades in accordance with specified parameters; (4) require
electric utilities, in establishing the capital plan, to evaluate bene-
fits of utilizing distributed energy resources such as energy storage or
managed charging programs; (5) define "future-proofing upgrades"; (6)
authorize the Commission, in consultation with the commissioner of envi-
ronmental conservation, to issue rules and regulations; (7) require the
Commission to identify and remove barriers to the efficient and timely
deployment of charging infrastructure needed to electrify New York's
commercial and public fleet vehicles and support charging deployment at
depots in the fleet charging zones, and in doing so, to consider a range
of specified factors; and (8) require capital plans to demonstrate
threshold labor standards.

§ 4: amends § 1020-gg of the public authorities law to require the Long
Island Power Authority (LIPA) to establish or amend an existing capital
plan to implement upgrades in its service territory in accordance with a
proceeding implemented by the public service commission pursuant to §
66-v of the public service law. LIPA and NYSERDA shall identify no fewer
than two highway charging hubs in LIPA's service territory where
future-proofing upgrades shall be implemented on a similar timeline as
at the thruway charging hubs defined in § 1885 of the public authorities
law.

§ 5. Establishes the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

New York has set rigorous goals - such as the Climate Leadership and
Community Protection Act of 2019 (CLCPA), Advanced Clean Trucks and
Advanced Clean Cars II rules, and the Zero Emissions Vehicles sales
targets - to predominantly electrify its transportation sector by 2050,
with significant target deadlines rapidly approaching. To meet the clean
transportation goals we have set, New York must now commit to equally
rigorous and well-planned goals to expedite electric grid transmission
and distribution infrastructure and interconnection upgrades. Fast
charging stations need to be built all along the New York State Thruway
and other high priority corridors. But fast chargers create considerable
demand for energy; exponentially more demand than currently required to
power the gas pumps found at Thruway rest stops and throughout the
state. As a result, as sales of zero emission vehicles continue to grow
and gain momentum, the electric grid must grow just as quickly to keep
pace with demand.

Electric grid infrastructure upgrades are costly and subject to a time-
consuming process that requires considerable coordination to plan, engi-
neer, permit, and construct. That extensive process must begin now - far
ahead of the electrification tar get deadlines - to meet the demands
that will emerge with those deadlines. In fact, if the upgrade process
fails to outpace the time when electric vehicle adoption reaches scale,
we will not have a reliable and adequate electric supply to power all
the new electric vehicles on New York's roadways.

This legislation establishes the framework to proactively plan for elec-
tric, vehicle fast-charging deployment on New York's highways by direct-
ing NYSERDA, in consultation with the Department of Transportation,
Department of Motor Vehicles, New York State Thruway Authority, New York
Power Authority, Long Island Power Authority, Department of Environ-
mental Conservation and the electric distribution and transmission util-
ities to, among other things, identify the number of fast chargers,
highway charging hubs, and fleet charging zones currently in operation
and in development along New York's priority highways, estimate future
need for fast charger deployment, and estimate total charging capacity
required through at least 2050. This planning will include stakeholder
input in line with existing energy planning processes, and NYSERDA will
then report the plan to the public service commission to effectuate it
through a proceeding that requires New York's electric utilities to
produce appropriate capital plans.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

TBD.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
